findings.claim: **Story-point estimation as commitment artefact, not prediction.** ... Either way the estimate is an artefact of the decision to commit, not a forecast. ... understanding its commitment-shape (versus its prediction-shape) is what stops it from becoming a serial overpromise pattern. (Source: Ch 2.5.5)
findings.failure_mode: Position the source does not hold, attributed to Ch 2.5.5; drives five later rows (68, 136, 175, 206)
findings.evidence: Deep ref line 87: ideal days = 'a number of days you think it'd take to complete the task'; teams make initial velocity estimates 'and adjust based on accuracy'. Source Ch 2.5.5 opens: estimation is 'figuring out ahead of time how long a task is likely to take'.
findings.fix: correct: **Story points and ideal days as calibrated estimates.** Story points compare task size to other tasks; ideal days estimate the days a task would take with no other tasks or distractions. Teams set an initial velocity and adjust it as they see how accurate their estimates were (Ch 2.5.5). For software-business commitments, that calibration loop is what keeps an estimate from becoming a serial overpromise.

findings.claim: Microservices as Conway's-Law-shaped team-and-capability decision ... each microservice can have its own tech stack and team boundary; decentralised governance means flexibility ... but increases coordination cost across teams. Conway's Law operates through this section even when not named: the architecture and the org chart will mirror each other.
findings.failure_mode: Smuggled concept with its own concept anchor (conways-law), plus a coordination-cost claim the source does not make
findings.evidence: No 'Conway' or 'coordinat' in source or deep ref. Deep ref line 205: 'each microservice can have its own tech stack (including its own database)'; line 209: decentralised governance means services 'need only be compatible at their interfaces', while a monolith team 'might only need to maintain a small set of technologies'. The anchor would route runtime Conway's-Law lookups to a source that never mentions it.
findings.fix: correct: retitle **Microservices organised around business capabilities**; keep the two [V] quotes and 'each microservice can have its own tech stack (including its own database)'; replace the coordination and Conway sentences with: decentralised governance leaves each service free in how it is implemented, while a monolith team might only need to maintain a small set of technologies (Ch 5.2.5). Drop the conways-law anchor.

findings.claim: Tuckman gives the model for why a new engineering team will not produce its eventual velocity for some weeks regardless of headcount — and therefore why a hiring decision made under commercial pressure needs a lead-time budget.
findings.failure_mode: Timing, velocity and headcount claims attributed to the Tuckman model as the source reports it
findings.evidence: Deep ref line 67 lists the five stages with no durations or productivity claims. Source 993-1017 adds only 'Consider where each [method] might fit in to these stages (there's not just one answer).'
findings.fix: correct: For software-business work, Tuckman's stages remind a leader that a newly formed team passes through Forming and Storming before it performs; plan for that when a commitment rests on a new team. (Label any lead-time estimate as the operator's, not Letaw's.)

findings.claim: The team has lost the distinction between estimate-as-commitment-artefact and estimate-as-forecast. Under pressure to be "right," the estimates will inflate ..., velocity will drop

findings.claim: Letaw is explicit that the book is method-level rather than theory-level or economics-level: it does not price software work in financial terms and does not carry empirical findings about software-engineering productivity, fault patterns, or estimation accuracy.
findings.failure_mode: Distillation's scope reading presented as the author's explicit statement
findings.evidence: Deep ref records Letaw's methods framing and curation stance (lines 13-15, 378) but no statement excluding theory or economics. The book does carry empirical figures (HPE survey, CHAOS failure rates; deep ref lines 17, 31), though none on productivity, faults or estimation accuracy.
findings.fix: correct: The book is method-level: it introduces 'a portable set of software engineering methods' (Introduction), does not price software work in financial terms, and carries no empirical findings on productivity, fault patterns or estimation accuracy (its data points are an adoption survey and CHAOS failure rates).

notes: Grading convention: a claim the source supports but the deep ref lacks is graded MINOR-DRIFT with a cycle-to-deep fix (D004, D005); UNSUPPORTED is kept for claims neither the deep ref nor the source supports. Three systemic defects: (1) 'twelve' code smells in seven places (plus '12 specific code smells' in the worked example), where source and deep ref give eleven; (2) the estimate-as-commitment-artefact-not-forecast stance, attributed to Ch 2.5.5, contradicts Letaw's definition of estimation and runs through Concept 5, a Phase 2 question, What to Look For, the worked example and an anti-pattern; (3) imported frames the source never uses: Conway's Law (with its own concept anchor, so a runtime Conway lookup lands here), Tuckman as a productivity-timeline model for hiring, and several integration rows crediting other sources with frameworks they do not hold (Mitchell-Agle-Wood in business ethics, Disagree-and-Commit in Liberating Structures, Mintzberg's six structures in Principles of Management). The borrowed-through list credits Microsoft with the Inclusivity Heuristics (GenderMag/OSU) and lists the held Scrum Guide as not held. Structure: the file adds a non-template section, 'When NOT to use this reference (route elsewhere)'; its Jones, accounting, principles-management, marketing and field-guide routings check out, the business-ethics one does not (D017). Verified word for word: RACI example, spike definition, 'organized around business capabilities', business-capability definition, TOCS deploy limit, MSM project-manager quote, refactoring definition, the three Ch 8.1 reason quotes, both requirement examples, 'can be converted to a scale', 'must only be stored on US servers', the constraints-vs-quality-attributes sentence, the five elicitation factors, 'one month or less', 'UML diagrams are for communicating with humans — not computers', 'geared toward Agile software development'.
